selected_topic.category: Kindle Store > Kindle eBooks > Romance > Contemporary > Small Town (verify the exact browse node in the KDP category picker; not confirmed).
selected_topic.description: Hannah Brooks has just returned to Cutter Street, the small Ohio town she left at eighteen, to take over her late grandmother's bakery. The shop is in debt, the oven is temperamental, and the one person who can fix the ovens is Eli Carver, the town's grumpy contractor who was her first crush and her grandmother's favorite fixer of everything. As they rebuild the bakery together, Hannah has to decide whether to sell the shop to a developer who has made a generous offer or keep it and the life she is starting to like. Eli has his own reasons for staying out of town politics. The story is warm, funny and romantic, with a close-knit cast of bakers, regulars and a dog who visits the shop every morning. It has no explicit sexual content, no profanity and no on-page violence. It ends with the bakery open, the developer defeated by the town and a hook for Book 2.
selected_topic.target_reader: Adult readers of sweet small-town romance who read on Kindle Unlimited, mostly women 30 to 60. They want a comforting love story with a clear happy ending and a strong sense of place.
selected_topic.royalty_tier: 70% tier (list price between $2.99 and $9.99). About $2.79 per sale before any delivery fee, which is negligible for a text-only file.
chapter_outline: 1. Opening Day: Hannah returns to the bakery and finds the oven dead and the cash box nearly empty.
2. The Man With the Wrench: Eli Carver arrives, unwilling, to look at the oven, and they clash over the repair bill.
3. Sourdough and Old Promises: Hannah finds her grandmother's notes and the history between her and Eli.
4. The Developer's Offer: a generous offer arrives, and the town begins to take sides.
5. Saturday Market: the bakery's first market stall brings regulars back and a new complication.
6. Late Nights in the Kitchen: Hannah and Eli work late, and the tension turns into friendship.
7. The Town Meeting: Eli is asked to speak against the developer, and he refuses.
8. The Winter Harvest: a storm damages the shop, and the town helps rebuild it.
9. A Letter From the Past: Hannah learns why her grandmother never sold the shop.
10. Open for Business: Hannah chooses the bakery and tells Eli how she feels.
11. Epilogue: First Snow: the shop is full, and a new visitor sets up Book 2.
selected_topic.tone_and_style: Warm, funny and cozy, with a light, observant voice. Close third person, past tense, alternating lightly between Hannah and Eli. Plain, concrete sentences, lots of food and place detail, and short chapters of about 2,500 words.

selected_topics.description: Margaret "Greta" Lowe spent thirty years as a court reporter, typing every word spoken in a courtroom on a stenotype machine. Now retired, she transcribes depositions from her lake-house kitchen in Lantern Bay, Michigan. At a stormy July meeting of the town council, Dale Whitcomb argues hard against the harbor lease, then dies the next morning in the harbor office. Deputy Sam Ortiz calls it natural causes. Greta's machine recorded every word, and the official minutes contain a sentence that was never spoken aloud. With eleven days before the council votes on the lease, Greta checks each transcript against the memories of the people in the room. Her allies are bookshop owner Priya Nand, retired fisherman Walt Brandt, and a gray cat named Judge who sleeps on her steno notes. The mystery turns on who rewrote the minutes and why. The book has no on-page violence, no explicit content and no profanity. It ends with the truth read aloud at a reconvened hearing and a hook for the next Lantern Bay case.
selected_topics.target_reader: Adult readers of cozy mysteries, mostly women 40 to 70, who read on Kindle Unlimited and want a clean, clever puzzle, a small-town cast and a series to follow.
selected_topics.royalty_tier: 70% (US list price between $2.99 and $9.99). About $2.75 per sale after the delivery fee (estimate).
chapter_outline: Last Call for Minutes: Greta transcribes the council meeting and notices her tape and the official minutes do not match.
Lantern Bay in July: Greta's routine, the cat Judge, and the town's split over the harbor lease.

The Bookshop Alibi: Greta and Priya Nand cross-check who was in the room and when they left.
The Fisherman's Story: Walt Brandt remembers a boat light and a second car parked behind the lease office.
A Note in the Mailbox: a warning arrives, and Greta realizes someone has been watching her house.
The Record Corrected: Greta reads the tape aloud at a reconvened hearing, and the room goes silent.
Lantern Bay Lights: the killer is exposed, the lease is decided, and Greta takes on the next case.
selected_topics.tone_and_style: Warm, witty and clean. Third person, past tense, close to Greta. No profanity, no explicit content and no on-page violence. Each chapter plants one fair clue for the reader to test, ends on a question, and balances cozy detail (food, weather, the cat) with a steady mystery pace. Use US English throughout.

selected_topics.description: Going back to school as an adult means balancing work and family with a brain that has not studied in years. This 30-day workbook teaches the study methods with the strongest research support: retrieval practice, spaced practice, interleaving and planning. Each chapter explains one method in plain language, shows a worked example from a returning student's week, and ends with prompts the reader answers in their own words. Readers finish with a personal weekly study plan, a note-taking system, a test-review routine and a 30-day habit tracker they can reuse for any course. This is general study guidance. It does not replace an academic advisor, a disability services office or an instructor.
selected_topics.target_reader: Adults aged 25 to 60 returning to community college, certificate programs, online courses or professional exams. They are busy, a little anxious about feeling behind, and want practical steps rather than theory.
selected_topics.royalty_tier: 70% (US list price between $2.99 and $9.99). About $3.45 per sale after the delivery fee (estimate).

Keep Going: habit tracking, asking for help, and a 30-day plan to reuse for the next course.
selected_topics.tone_and_style: Encouraging, plain-spoken and practical. Second person, present tense, one method per chapter, a worked example, then prompts. Every research claim is tied to a named source in metadata.json (Dunlosky et al., 2013; Roediger and Karpicke, 2006; Cepeda et al., 2006). Include the general-information disclaimer. No clinical, medical or legal advice and no promises about grades. Avoid learning-styles claims. Use US English throughout.

selected_topics.description: Tessa Marsh inherits her late uncle's home-staging business in Larkspur Lake, Wisconsin, a small resort town that comes alive every summer when the lake cottages go on the market. On the first morning, she pulls into the Birch Street cottage and finds a rival stager already unloading a cream sofa on the lawn, the same sofa she has brought for the same open house. The rival is Owen Reyes, a local realtor who has been quietly using her uncle's old props in his own listings. The two agree to split the Birch Street job and immediately start to bicker over every lamp, rug and throw pillow. As the summer goes on, their rivalry turns into a partnership, and then into something neither of them planned. Tessa has to decide whether to sell the business and go back to Chicago or to stay and build something of her own. The story is witty, warm and romantic, with a close-knit lake-town cast, a family dog and a clear happy ending. It has no explicit sexual content, no profanity and no on-page violence.
selected_topics.target_reader: Adult readers of contemporary romantic comedy, mostly women 28 to 55, who read on Kindle Unlimited and want a witty, warm love story with a clear happy ending and a strong sense of place.

Closing Day and the Epilogue: Tessa chooses Larkspur Lake and tells Owen the truth, and the last scene sets up Book 2.

selected_topics.description: Ten Stitches, Thirty Days teaches adults who are new to hand embroidery one stitch at a time. Readers learn which tools and fabrics to buy, how to transfer a design onto fabric, and ten core stitches: running, backstitch, straight, stem, split, chain, satin, French knot, lazy daisy and blanket stitch. Each stitch has numbered steps, a short list of common mistakes and a 15-minute practice session in a thirty-day schedule that builds gradually. The book ends with a hoop sampler that uses all ten stitches as a finished project. The self-help angle is steady, low-pressure practice and a routine that fits a busy week. It makes no health or mood promises. This is general craft instruction, not professional advice, and every stitch name and step is checked against a named source.
selected_topics.target_reader: Adults 25 to 65 who want a calm, hands-on hobby, gift makers, and people who tried embroidery once and want a clear, patient starting point.
selected_topics.royalty_tier: 70% (US list price between $2.99 and $12.99). About $3.39 per sale after the delivery fee (estimate: a 1 MB file at $0.15 per MB).
chapter_outline: Before the Needle: the tools, fabrics, hoops and threads a beginner needs.
Transferring a Design: tracing methods, water-soluble markers and choosing fabric.

Stem, Split and Chain: curves, outlines and textured lines.

Fixing Mistakes Without Tears: unpicking, tension and puckering.
Thirty Days of Practice: the daily schedule, with one short session per day.
The Hoop Sampler: a finished project that uses all ten stitches.
selected_topics.tone_and_style: Clear, encouraging and practical. Second person (you), present tense, one point of view throughout. Short numbered steps in plain language. Every stitch name, step and tool description is checked against a named source during drafting. Includes the non-fiction general-information disclaimer. No health, mood or stress-relief claims unless sourced.
